newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Albright takes tough line from Croatia to Serbia.
newsitem.headline: Albright takes tough line from Croatia to Serbia.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright showed rare undiplomatic bluntness on Saturday when she publicly faulted the presidents of Croatia and Serbia for inactivity and threatened sanctions unless they changed.

After an open spat with Croatian President Franjo Tudjman, Albright held talks with Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic in Belgrade on subjects including Bosnia war crimes, the return of refugees and Serbia's troubling trend on political liberties.
Milosevic opened the 90-minute meeting by telling reporters he wanted to normalise relations with the United States.

But Albright made clear at a news conference later that clear this goal was not close to being realised. She accused Milosevic of dragging his feet on apprehending war criminals and other commitments and warned that Serbia was "at a fork in the road."

"I assured him that (if Serbia fails to meet U.S. demands) the United States would make sure they are not part of the dynamic trend that was taking place in Europe and that they would be left far behind," she said.

Albright said her session with Milosevic "was probably the toughest meeting I've had with any president," adding: "I made clear to President Milosevic that it now was up to him if there would be steps toward normalisation."

She called for Milosevic, a key signatory of the 1995 U.S.- brokered Dayton accords that ended the Bosnia war, to stop "stonewalling" and ensure that indicated war criminals were brought to justice at the war crimes Tribunal in The Hague.
She specifically cited influential Bosnian Serb Radovan Karadzic and three Yugoslav generals accused of a mass killing near Vukovar.
Milosevic claimed he did not have enough information about the three generals but Albright said she gave him tribunal documents so "he has no excuses."
She also urged him to bring to trial in Serbia a Serb military leader known as Arkan, her spokesman Nicholas Burns said. But he said the meeting produced no progress on any issue.
Milosevic told reporters after the meeting that the talks were very open and "in the spirit of tradition between our two countries in their long history."
"I am certain that we will achieve better and better progress as regards the questions we discussed and normalise our relations step by step," he said.

Albright later walked to the Czech embassy near the Serbian presidency buildings to the amazement of onlookers who almost never see high officials walking the streets. She lived in the embassy as a child when her father was a diplomat in Belgrade.
Albright, who flaunts a "tell it like it is" diplomacy, had a tough meeting with Tudjman earlier in Zagreb and a direct face-off at a joint news conference.

As Tudjman looked on grim-faced, she said: "I believe it is the appropriate role of leadership of every country to provide moral direction ... and I asked President Tudjman to provide that kind of leadership."

She said she told Tudjman, who is up for re-election in two weeks time, that he must prevent violence against Serb war refugees trying to return to Croatia and also cooperate with the war crimes tribunal at the Hague.

Albright told him that if he failed to act on U.S. demands, which include commitments he made as a signatory of the Dayton accords, Washington would block International Monetary Fund loans and Croatia's integration into the western community.

Her spokesman told reporters the only commitment Tudjman made was to open the bridge at Brcko over the Sava River from the Bosnian Serb republic to Croatia to trade. Albright is to visit Brcko on Sunday.

Tudjman insisted Zagreb supported the right of Serbs to return to his country and was complying with other aspects of the Dayton accords. "For all practical purposes Croatia is not operating any programme of ethnic purity," he said.
